tip: With a different subject, чтобы (chtoby) needs a past-form verb, not an infinitive: сказал, чтобы мы открыли (skazal, chtoby my atkryli = told us to open).
по (po) plus the dative plural means 'every' or 'on': по вечерам (po vecheram = in the evenings) marks a regular, repeated action.
либо ... либо (liba ... liba = either ... or) is the paired 'either/or', a touch more formal than или (ili).
тот, кто (tot, kto) means he who: the pointer тот (tot = that one) leads and the relative кто (kto = who) opens the clause.
In reported questions Russian keeps the original tense: живу (zhivu = live) stays present after спросила (sprasila = asked), where English might shift to lived.
с (s = with) takes the instrumental case, so молоко (malako) becomes молоком (malakom): чай с молоком (chai s malakom = tea with milk).
пока не (paka ne = until) marks the point an action lasts up to. The не (ne) here is not a negation: стемнело (stemnela = it got dark) is a real event.
если (esli = if) here is a real condition. For an unreal one use если бы plus a past verb: если бы ты хотел (esli by ty khatel = if you wanted).
As a conjunction раз (raz) means since or given that, a casual way to give a reason: раз ты здесь (raz ty zdes = since you are here).
The imperfective past читал (chital = used to read) covers repeated action, so with каждый день (kazhdy den = every day) it means read habitually.
надела (nadela = put on) comes from надеть (nadet), for putting clothes on yourself. одеть (adet) means to dress someone else. платье (plate = dress) takes надеть.
куда (kuda = to where) marks direction with a motion verb like едем (edem = we go). Use где (gde = where) only for a fixed location.
сказали (skazali = told) with no subject plus dative мне (mne = to me) is Russian's they-told-me, standing in for the English passive I was told.
After как только (kak tolka = as soon as) Russian uses a future verb: освобожусь (asvabazhus = I will be free), where English keeps the present.
The verb бояться (bayatsya = to fear) takes the genitive, so the relative is чего (chevo), not что (chto): то, чего я боялся (to, chevo ya bayalsya = what I feared).
так что (tak chto = so, therefore) marks a result: уехали, так что дом пустой (uekhali, tak chto dom pustoy). For a cause use так как (tak kak) instead.
The frame как ... так и (kak ... tak i) means both...and: как дети, так и взрослые (kak deti, tak i vzroslye = both children and adults).
Paired не только ... но и (ne tolka ... no i) means not only...but also: не только он, но и она (ne tolka on, no i ana = not only he, but she).
как бы ... ни (kak by ... ni) means no matter how: как бы трудно ни было (kak by trudna ni byla = however hard it is). The ни (ni) is not a negation.
чтобы (chtoby) marks a wish or command and takes a past-tense verb: чтобы мы были (chtoby my byli = that we be). Plain что (chto = that) only reports a fact.
The preposition stays in front of который: по которому (pa katoramu = along which). Russian keeps по and который together as one phrase.
без (bez = without) takes the genitive case, so сахар (sakhar) shifts to сахара (sakhara) here.
For a time of day Russian uses the instrumental with no preposition: вечером (vecheram = in the evening).
до (do = until, up to) takes the genitive, so вечер (vecher) becomes вечера (vechera) here.
For weather, идти (idti) means 'to fall': шёл снег (shyol sneg = snow was falling), literally 'snow went'.
через (cherez = through) plus a time span means 'after, in': через час (cherez chas = in an hour).
из (iz = out of) takes the genitive, so магазин (magazin) becomes магазина (magazina) for 'from where'.
к (k = toward) takes the dative and is the 'to' used for people: к врачу (k vrachu = to the doctor).
несмотря на (nesmatrya na = despite) takes the accusative: несмотря на дождь (... na dozhd = despite the rain).
во время (vo vremya = during) takes the genitive, so урок (urok) becomes урока (uroka) here.
